intro_cards.title: What this is about
intro_cards.body:
Rules in a building code are applied by people and, increasingly, by software. Both have to settle details that the text of the code does not spell out. We want to learn how you settle some of them.

Please answer as you would in your own work. **There is no expected right answer.** "Depends" is a valuable answer: choose it whenever the answer depends on something not stated, and tell us on what.

intro_cards.title: How the cards work
intro_cards.body: The clause text is available under the book symbol on every card. Some cards ask a general question. Others describe a case: one situation in which only the stated points differ from a plain, otherwise compliant design. Whatever a case does not mention is as it should be. Cards that belong together are linked and show your earlier answer.

sections.title: Stair handrails (4.7.3.1)
sections.question: Is the handrail in this case in accordance with clause 4.7.3.1(b)?

cards.prompt: Clause 4.7.3.1 states the handrail requirements without mentioning a number of steps. In practice, are they limited to stairs above a certain number of steps?

options.label: Yes, limited to stairs above a certain number of steps
options.detail: Please name the number in the note.

options.label: No, they apply to every stair

follow_up.label: Number of steps and the document or wording it comes from, if you know it (optional)

cards.prompt: A requirement is limited to stairs with more than a stated number of steps. For a flight of stairs, are the steps counted by its risers or by its treads?
cards.hint: A flight that begins and ends at a floor or landing level has one tread fewer than it has risers.

options.label: By its risers
options.detail: The number of risers is compared with the stated number.

options.label: By its treads
options.detail: The number of treads is compared with the stated number.

cards.prompt: A requirement is limited to stairs with more than a stated number of steps. A stair has two flights joined by an intermediate landing. Which count is compared with the stated number?

options.label: The count of the whole stair
options.detail: The steps of both flights are added together.

options.label: The count of each flight, separately
options.detail: Each flight is judged on its own count.

cards.prompt: Note 1 to clause 4.7.1.1 says that clause 4.7.1.1 does not apply within residential units. Clause 4.7.1.1(b) refers to clause 4.7.3 for stair handrails. For a stair inside a residential unit, for example a stair between the two storeys of one maisonette, is the handrail height of 4.7.3.1(b) checked?

options.label: No, the height is not checked

cards.prompt: Clause 4.7.3.1(b) asks for a handrail "between 800 mm and 1000 mm" above the pitch line. A handrail measured at exactly 800 mm, or at exactly 1000 mm, is:

options.label: Compliant at both limits
options.detail: 800 mm and 1000 mm are inside the range.

options.label: Compliant at neither limit
options.detail: 800 mm and 1000 mm are outside the range.

options.label: Compliant at one limit only
options.detail: Please say which in the note.

cards.title: Two flights, one handrail at 700 mm
cards.assumption: The stair is in the common area of an office building, not within a residential unit. Every other requirement of clause 4.7.3.1 is met.
changes: A stair connects two floors. It has two straight flights of ==4 risers== each, joined by an intermediate landing: 8 risers in total.
The handrail along the first flight has its top ==700 mm== above the pitch line, measured vertically. The handrail along the second flight is at 900 mm.

figure.alt: Side view of two flights of four risers with a landing; handrail at 700 mm on the first flight and 900 mm on the second.
figure.caption: Side view, not to scale — height measured vertically from pitch line to handrail

sections.title: Bollards (4.2.3.6)
sections.question: Does the bollard in this case comply with clause 4.2.3.6(c)?

cards.prompt: Clause 4.2.3.6 applies where bollards are erected at entrances to walkways or pathways. Clause 3.2.2 says that where bollards are used, clause 4.2.3.6 applies. Does the minimum height of 800 mm in 4.2.3.6(c) apply to a bollard that does not stand at an entrance to a walkway or pathway?

options.label: No, it does not apply
options.detail: The 800 mm minimum is not required by this clause.

cards.prompt: Clause 4.2.3.6(c) gives a minimum height of 800 mm. A bollard stands on a paved area that slopes along the bollard, so the paving at its base is higher on one side than on the other. From which level is the height measured?

options.label: Paving level at the centre of the bollard's base
options.detail: The level directly below the axis of the bollard.

options.label: Highest paving level at the base
Lowest paving level at the base

cards.title: A 700 mm bollard at the far corner of a plaza
cards.assumption: The two bollards at the start of the footpath are 900 mm high and meet every other requirement of 4.2.3.6.
changes: A paved plaza of 4 m × 4 m has a footpath, 1.5 m wide, leaving from one side.
Two bollards stand at the start of the footpath. A third bollard, ==700 mm== high, stands at the far corner of the plaza, about 4 m from the nearest of the two.

figure.alt: Plan of a plaza and a footpath. Two 900 mm bollards stand at the footpath start; a 700 mm bollard stands at the far plaza corner.
figure.caption: Plan — H = vertical bollard height above paving; 4.00 m / 1.50 m are plan sizes

closing.title: Finally
closing.free_text_label: Which decisions in applying these two clauses did we not ask about, but a checker should settle explicitly? Any other remarks?
